planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; Nash's meadow beauty is taller and more robust than most Rhexia species and colonizes readily by rhizomes once sited in permanently damp, nutrient-poor ground.

directions: Site in constantly moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), sandy or peaty soil in full sun to light partial shade, ideally along a pond margin, rain garden low spot, or seasonally flooded ditch. Nash's meadow beauty is a coastal-plain native ranging from New Jersey to Florida and west to Louisiana, growing among maidencane and other wet-savanna grasses in marsh edges and shallow roadside swales. It forms upright, hairy-stemmed clumps taller than most of its relatives and produces showy four-petaled, deep rose-purple flowers with curved yellow anthers from midsummer into early fall, followed by the urn-shaped seed capsules typical of the genus. Like other meadow beauties it depends on buzz-pollinating bumblebees to release its pollen, and it spreads gradually by shallow rhizomes to form loose colonies in consistently wet, acidic ground; it will not persist in average garden soil that dries out or contains lime.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Eco Lacquered Spider' spreads quickly by wiry, above-ground stolons and roots readily wherever a node touches moist soil, filling in as a dense groundcover within a season or two.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled woodland light; this selection tolerates more sun in cooler climates if kept consistently watered. 'Eco Lacquered Spider' was selected and introduced by plantsman Don Jacobs of Eco Gardens in Georgia for its glossy, dark green, bronze-tinged foliage and unusually vigorous, far-reaching stolons that radiate out from the crown like spider legs, rooting as they go to knit together a dense, weed-suppressing mat faster than the species. Cheerful five-petaled bright yellow daisy flowers appear in flushes from mid-spring through early summer with sporadic rebloom into fall. It is an excellent low-maintenance native groundcover for shaded slopes, woodland-garden edges, and beneath deciduous shrubs, and provides early-season pollen and nectar for small native bees.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Marsh Obedient Plant (Gulf Coast False Dragonhead)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; marsh obedient plant is native to Gulf Coast wet pinelands and spreads steadily by rhizomes when kept damp, making it well suited to rain gardens and pond margins.

directions: Grow in reliably moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade; marsh obedient plant is a specialist of wet pine savannas, roadside ditches, and freshwater marsh edges along the Gulf coastal plain from Louisiana and Mississippi through the Florida panhandle. It bears narrow, willowy leaves and upright spikes of tubular, pale lavender-pink flowers spotted with deeper purple in the throat from late summer into fall, and like its better-known relative Physostegia virginiana, individual flowers can be pushed sideways on the spike and will hold their new position - the trait that gives the genus its common name. It spreads by shallow rhizomes to form colonies in consistently damp ground and is an excellent choice for the wet fringes of a rain garden or pond where taller, showier perennials tend to struggle; it declines quickly if the soil is allowed to dry out.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold-moist stratification over winter, or cold-stratify 60-90 days before spring sowing; meadow zizia establishes well in rich, humusy woodland-edge soil and self-seeds modestly once established.

directions: Plant in rich, humusy, well-drained to evenly moist soil in partial shade to dappled sun, mimicking the open woodland edges, rocky slopes, and streamside meadows of the southern Appalachians and Piedmont where it grows wild from Pennsylvania south into Georgia and Alabama. Meadow zizia is distinguished from the more common golden Alexanders (Zizia aurea) by its compound, three-parted (ternate) leaflets rather than pinnately divided leaves, and it tends to favor shadier, drier woodland-edge sites rather than open wet meadows. Flat-topped clusters of small, bright yellow flowers open in mid-spring atop wiry stems, offering an early nectar source for small bees and flies, and the foliage serves as a larval host plant for black swallowtail butterflies just as other Zizia species do. It is a graceful, underused native for the partial-shade wildflower garden and pairs well with other spring ephemerals along a woodland path.

planting.note: Plant divisions or dormant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; Florida bellwort spreads slowly by rhizomes into a loose colony and is best left undisturbed once established beneath a deciduous canopy.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath hardwood canopy; Florida bellwort is a warm-climate specialist restricted to rich wooded bluffs, ravine slopes, and floodplain forests of the Florida panhandle, southern Georgia, and southern Alabama, ranging much farther south than most other Uvularia species. It produces the same nodding, twisted, pale yellow bell-shaped flowers typical of the genus in early to mid-spring, held above perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, followed by attractive three-angled seed capsules. Clumps spread gradually by short rhizomes to form loose colonies over years rather than aggressively covering ground, making it well suited to a shaded native plant collection or woodland garden that mimics the calcareous bluff forests of the Deep South. It combines beautifully with trilliums, wild ginger, and other spring-flowering shade natives that share its habitat.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown starts in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; 'Callaway' forms a slowly expanding evergreen clump and should be left undisturbed once established, needing only occasional division to propagate.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; 'Callaway' resents drying out and heavy clay but otherwise asks little once its leaf-litter mulch is renewed each fall. This selection of the southeastern native mottled wild ginger was named for Callaway Gardens in Pine Mountain, Georgia, where it was found and propagated for its notably large, heart-shaped, leathery evergreen leaves heavily marbled with silver-gray, a more dramatic and vigorous form than typical wild-collected Hexastylis shuttleworthii. The small, jug-shaped, maroon-brown flowers are borne low at ground level in spring, hidden beneath the foliage and pollinated by ground-dwelling beetles and flies rather than showy pollinators. It is prized as an evergreen groundcover for shaded rock gardens and woodland borders, slowly forming a handsome weed-suppressing patch that holds its glossy mottled leaves through winter.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox
